content: Decentralizing services, while increasing costs for service providers, governments, donor agencies, and insurance systems, can significantly reduce expenses for users. This is because users will need to travel less and spend less time away from their homes or jobs, leading to potential savings and increased earnings. These factors must be carefully considered when evaluating the overall cost of decentralizing services. Bringing services closer to users is not only more practical but can also yield economic benefits for society. Additionally, decentralized services can improve repair and maintenance processes, extending the lifespan of prostheses and orthoses and reducing the cost of replacements. A satellite service unit is a small facility located in a decentralized area, ideally integrated into a hospital or health center to facilitate collaboration with healthcare personnel. Initially, these units may not be permanently staffed but can be visited regularly, such as every 2–3 weeks, by personnel from a main service unit. These satellite units are equipped to take measurements, create casts, fit devices, and perform repairs and maintenance on prostheses and orthoses, while relying on the main center for fabrication. Starting on a small scale, satellite units can expand and increase the frequency of visits as they become more recognized in the area and as demand for services grows. Over time, these units may evolve into permanent facilities. At an intermediate stage, they may be staffed by physiotherapists, occupational therapists, nurses, or trained community-based rehabilitation (CBR) workers who can conduct initial screenings and prepare users for treatment. Alternatively, they may be staffed by prosthetics and orthotics technicians who can perform repairs and maintenance. To enhance decentralization, a main unit may oversee several satellite units. Despite differences in staffing, satellite units must adhere to the same standards as the overall service system. Mobile prosthetics and orthotics units are essentially service facilities on wheels or, in some countries, on boats. These units are equipped with the necessary tools and machinery to produce a range of prostheses and orthoses and are staffed by a multidisciplinary team, ideally including prosthetics and orthotics specialists, doctors, therapists, and social or CBR workers. Mobile units are particularly useful in remote areas, often in collaboration with district or sub-district hospitals and primary healthcare centers, to identify needs, deliver services, refer users to secondary units, and provide follow-up care. They can also raise awareness about prosthetics and orthotics services, increasing demand and paving the way for the establishment of permanent service units. Mobile units can operate independently in wide areas for extended periods, provided they have sufficient materials and staff compensation for fieldwork conditions. However, mobile services are often more expensive than fixed facilities due to vehicle costs and higher personnel expenses for allowances and accommodations. To remain cost-effective, mobile units should stay in one location only as long as their capacity is fully utilized and ensure that all treatments adhere to standard procedures. Some cases may need to be referred to a main unit due to complexity or lengthy treatment requirements. Mobile services must meet the same quality standards as main units and follow well-defined procedures to ensure high-quality care. Outreach services, often organized in emergencies or to reach very remote populations, involve a series of visits to a location, ideally in collaboration with district or sub-district hospitals or primary healthcare centers. These services are provided by a team similar to that of a mobile unit but without most of the tools and machinery. During the first visit, potential users are screened, assessed, and measured, with casts made or prefabricated devices provided. Custom-made products are fabricated at the service unit and fitted during a second visit. Follow-up visits may be conducted by the team or community workers. Outreach services can also include limited maintenance and repair of devices. In some countries, simple prosthetic and orthotic products may be manufactured on-site. The main challenge of outreach services is ensuring the quality of treatment and products, as they are often provided under time constraints, with limited equipment, and in environments that may not support standard procedures or user privacy. These services should only be provided when monitoring, evaluation, and follow-up confirm that they meet quality requirements. Most users, particularly those requiring training and close follow-up, are referred to a service unit for treatment. Community-based rehabilitation (CBR) programs play a crucial role in ensuring that a large proportion of people with disabilities receive rehabilitation within their communities. CBR workers can identify individuals with disabilities, conduct basic functional assessments, provide simple rehabilitation treatments, train family members to support individuals with disabilities, and facilitate referrals to specialized rehabilitation services, including prosthetics and orthotics. They can also follow up with users upon their return. CBR programs raise community awareness about disability, rehabilitation, and prosthetics and orthotics services, making them important partners for service providers. Basic prosthetics and orthotics treatments may be provided by community workers, but only if they have received sufficient training and their work is closely supervised. It is essential to clearly define the roles and limitations of community workers and the circumstances under which they should consult specialists at prosthetics and orthotics units. Telemedicine and telerehabilitation use information and communication technology to provide clinical services remotely, particularly in areas where face-to-face consultations are difficult or expensive. These technologies can facilitate access to generalists or specialists and support healthcare personnel in managing rare or complex conditions locally. Data and images can be stored and transmitted or used for real-time consultations. Telerehabilitation applies these technologies to rehabilitation services, improving access for individuals with physical impairments or functional limitations. This allows for more specialized interventions and follow-up care at the local level. To be effective, telerehabilitation technology should be lightweight, user-friendly, and capable of real-time communication. Lessons from telemedicine and telerehabilitation can be applied to prosthetics and orthotics services, particularly in outreach screening, specialist assessments, and user follow-up. In the Philippines, for example, the Amputee Screening through Cellphone Networking (ASCENT) program uses mobile technology to screen amputees in remote areas, demonstrating the potential of such approaches in reaching underserved communities.
